## Warm-Up: Quick Concept and Calculation Checks

a. If real GDP is temporarily *above* potential GDP, what eventually happens to nominal wages, and
   which direction does SRAS shift as a result?
b. If real GDP is temporarily *below* potential GDP, what eventually happens to nominal wages
   (even though this happens slowly), and which direction does SRAS shift as a result?
c. On the short-run Phillips curve, is the relationship between unemployment and inflation
   positive or negative?
d. Is the long-run Phillips curve upward sloping, downward sloping, or vertical? At what
   unemployment rate does it sit?
e. If unemployment is temporarily below the natural rate and inflation is rising, is this a
   short-run or a long-run Phillips curve situation?
f. Why does the short-run unemployment-inflation tradeoff eventually disappear as expected
   inflation catches up to actual inflation?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. Nominal wages eventually *rise* (firms compete for workers in a tight labor market), which
   shifts SRAS *left*.
b. Nominal wages eventually *fall*, though slowly since wages are sticky downward, which shifts
   SRAS *right*.
c. *Negative* (inverse): lower unemployment tends to come with higher inflation, and vice versa.
d. *Vertical*, at the *natural rate of unemployment*.
e. *Short-run*. The long run is defined by the economy having fully adjusted back to the natural
   rate of unemployment, regardless of the inflation rate.
f. Once expected inflation rises to match actual inflation, the short-run Phillips curve itself
   shifts, and the temporary tradeoff vanishes, unemployment drifts back toward the natural rate
   even if inflation remains elevated.

</details>

## Problem 1: Self-Correction After an Inflationary Gap

An economy's potential GDP is 400 (illustrative units). AD is fixed at $AD(P) = 600 - 4(P-90)$.
The original short-run supply curve is $SRAS_0(P) = 400 + 4(P-90)$.

a. Find the short-run equilibrium price level and real GDP where $AD(P) = SRAS_0(P)$.
b. Is this equilibrium's real GDP above, below, or equal to potential GDP? What is this gap
   called?
c. Over time, self-correction shifts the supply curve to $SRAS_1(P) = 200 + 4(P-90)$. Find the new
   equilibrium where $AD(P) = SRAS_1(P)$.
d. Compare the new equilibrium's real GDP to potential GDP. What happened to the price level
   between the two equilibria?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"
GREEN = "#548235"
RED = "#c00000"

P = list(range(85, 145, 5))
AD = [600 - 4*(p-90) for p in P]
SRAS0 = [400 + 4*(p-90) for p in P]
SRAS1 = [200 + 4*(p-90) for p in P]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=AD, y=P, mode="lines", name="AD", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=SRAS0, y=P, mode="lines", name="SRAS (original)",
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=2, dash="dot")))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=SRAS1, y=P, mode="lines", name="SRAS (after self-correction)",
                          line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[400, 400], y=[85, 145], mode="lines", name="LRAS (potential = 400)",
                          line=dict(color=GREEN, width=2, dash="dash")))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[500], y=[115], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=12, color="black"),
                          showlegend=False))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[400], y=[140], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=12, color=RED),
                          showlegend=False))
fig.update_layout(xaxis_title="Real GDP", yaxis_title="Price level",
                  width=620, height=440, plot_bgcolor="white",
                  legend=dict(x=0.02, y=1.25, orientation="h", font=dict(size=9)))
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.show()
```

a. Setting $600-4(P-90)=400+4(P-90)$: $200=8(P-90) \Rightarrow P-90=25 \Rightarrow P=115$. Real GDP
   $= 400+4(25)=500$.
b. Real GDP (500) is *above* potential GDP (400). This is an *inflationary gap*.
c. Setting $600-4(P-90)=200+4(P-90)$: $400=8(P-90) \Rightarrow P-90=50 \Rightarrow P=140$. Real GDP
   $=200+4(50)=400$.
d. The new equilibrium's real GDP (400) now exactly *equals* potential GDP, the economy has fully
   self-corrected. The price level *rose*, from 115 to 140, and settled permanently higher, exactly
   the pattern predicted: an inflationary gap closes through rising nominal wages, shrinking SRAS,
   and a higher long-run price level, not through any change in long-run output.

</details>

## Problem 2: Reading the Short-Run Phillips Curve

A short-run Phillips curve is given by the relationship: inflation rate $= 10 - u$, where $u$ is
the unemployment rate (in percent). The natural rate of unemployment in this economy is 5 percent.

a. What is the inflation rate when unemployment is 4 percent?
b. What is the inflation rate when unemployment is 8 percent?
c. What is the inflation rate when unemployment is exactly at the natural rate (5 percent)?
d. Explain why this same short-run Phillips curve is really just another way of drawing the
   demand-pull side of the AD/AS model from Chapter 12.

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"

u = list(range(2, 11))
inflation = [10 - x for x in u]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=u, y=inflation, mode="lines", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
                          hovertemplate="Unemployment %{x}%<br>Inflation %{y}%<extra></extra>"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[5], y=[5], mode="markers", marker=dict(size=11, color="black"),
                          showlegend=False))
fig.update_layout(xaxis_title="Unemployment rate (percent)", yaxis_title="Inflation rate (percent)",
                  width=520, height=380, plot_bgcolor="white", showlegend=False)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.show()
```

a. Inflation $= 10 - 4 = 6$ percent.
b. Inflation $= 10 - 8 = 2$ percent.
c. Inflation $= 10 - 5 = 5$ percent.
d. Higher AD (demand-pull inflation) both raises the price level *and* raises real GDP, which
   means more hiring and *lower* unemployment. The same underlying demand-pull story that raises
   the price level and real GDP together in the AD/AS model also raises inflation while lowering
   unemployment, just plotted on different axes.

</details>

## Problem 3: When Expected Inflation Rises

A short-run Phillips curve is $\pi = \pi^e - (u - 5)$, where $\pi$ is actual inflation, $u$ is the
unemployment rate (in percent), $\pi^e$ is expected inflation, and 5 percent is the natural rate of
unemployment.

a. If expected inflation $\pi^e = 3$ percent, what is actual inflation when unemployment is exactly
   at the natural rate (5 percent)?
b. Still with $\pi^e = 3$ percent, suppose the economy overheats and unemployment falls to 3
   percent. What is actual inflation now?
c. Now suppose expected inflation has risen to $\pi^e = 6$ percent (people have come to expect more
   inflation, based on recent experience), with unemployment still at 3 percent. What is actual
   inflation?
d. Compare your answers to (b) and (c). What happened to the short-run Phillips curve itself as
   expected inflation rose? At the natural rate of unemployment, does actual inflation ever differ
   from expected inflation in this model?

<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. $\pi = 3 - (5-5) = 3 - 0 = 3$ percent. At the natural rate, the $(u-5)$ term is zero, so actual
   inflation simply equals expected inflation.
b. $\pi = 3 - (3-5) = 3 + 2 = 5$ percent. With unemployment *below* the natural rate, actual
   inflation runs *above* expected inflation, the short-run tradeoff at work.
c. $\pi = 6 - (3-5) = 6 + 2 = 8$ percent.
d. Comparing (b) and (c), at the *same* unemployment rate (3 percent), actual inflation rose from 5
   to 8 percent, exactly the 3 percentage point rise in expected inflation. The entire short-run
   Phillips curve *shifted up* by that amount. And at the natural rate of unemployment specifically,
   actual inflation always exactly equals expected inflation, whatever that happens to be, there is
   no stable, exploitable tradeoff there: unemployment cannot be held permanently below the natural
   rate just by tolerating ever-higher inflation, once expectations catch up, only inflation ends up
   permanently higher, not unemployment permanently lower.

</details>
